planting.note: Direct sow in spring onto loose, bare, well-drained sand in full sun; this sedge germinates readily on disturbed or blown-out sand and struggles once grasses close in around it.

directions: Schweinitz's flatsedge is a true sand specialist found on open dunes and blowouts across the Nebraska Sandhills and central Great Plains, where its pale, wiry, grass-like foliage and spreading rhizomes help knit together loose, shifting sand that few other sedges can tolerate. Flattened, straw-colored flower clusters appear atop short stems in mid- to late summer, giving it a subtle, textural presence rather than a showy one. It is best used in restoration plantings or sand-prairie gardens on bare, lean, fast-draining sand, since richer or more stable soil quickly lets taller competitors crowd it out. Skip fertilizer and supplemental water entirely once plants are established.
sources: Flora of the Great Plains, Great Plains Flora Association

planting.note: Fall sow onto lean, well-drained sandy to loamy upland soil in full sun to let winter cold-moist stratification break seed dormancy; established clumps resent heavy, wet, or richly fertilized ground.

directions: Threadleaf sedge forms tight, fine-textured tufts of hair-thin, evergreen-gray foliage across the drier upland swales and sandy ridges of the Nebraska and Kansas Sandhills mixed-grass prairie, filling the low, ground-hugging niche beneath taller bunchgrasses like sand bluestem and little bluestem. Its inconspicuous brownish flower spikes appear in late spring, but the plant earns its place through year-round structure and its extreme tolerance of drought, wind, and grazing. It spreads slowly from a dense, fibrous crown rather than running aggressively, making it well suited to lean, unirrigated native plantings, dry rock gardens, or shortgrass-style lawn substitutes. Avoid shade, heavy soil, and supplemental irrigation, all of which cause it to thin out and decline.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto loose, lean, sandy soil in full sun so winter cold and moisture can break seed dormancy; this short-lived species reseeds readily on open sand but fades out once the ground vegetates over.

directions: Whitest evening primrose is a low, sprawling annual to short-lived perennial of open sand prairie and blowouts across the Nebraska and Kansas Sandhills, with finely cut gray-green leaves and large, pure white, four-petaled flowers that open in the evening and fade to pink by the following afternoon. It thrives on bare, loose, nutrient-poor sand and depends on at least some open ground to reseed itself each year, so it works best scattered among sparser native grasses rather than packed into a dense perennial border. The flowers draw hawk moths and other evening pollinators during their brief nightly bloom. Give it full sun and skip fertilizer and extra water, both of which favor taller competitors over this low sand specialist.
sources: Flora of the Great Plains, Great Plains Flora Association

planting.note: Fall sow onto loose, lean, well-drained sandy soil in full sun to allow winter stratification; silver bladderpod forms a basal rosette the first year and typically flowers the following spring.

directions: Silver bladderpod is a low, silvery-haired rosette-forming perennial of open sand prairie and dune slopes across the Nebraska and Kansas Sandhills and the central Great Plains, its dense coat of fine hairs reflecting intense sun and giving the foliage a soft, frosted look year-round. Small, four-petaled yellow flowers crowd short stalks above the rosette in early spring, followed by the small, inflated, bladder-like seed pods that give the plant its common name. It requires bare, loose, fast-draining sand and full sun, declining quickly in rich garden soil or where grasses crowd in around it. Once established on an open, unirrigated sandy site it needs no fertilizer and tolerates extended drought without decline.
sources: Flora of the Great Plains, Great Plains Flora Association
